## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Fundamentals of Reproducible Research and Free Software
  Official title       Fondamentaux de la recherche reproductible et du logiciel libre / Fundamentals of reproducible research and free software
  Instructors          M. COLOM BARCO (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 12 h, tutorials 3 h, labs 9 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label}[Track RR]{.badge .track}
  Language             not displayed; the course description on master-mva.com is written in English
  Assessment           Each group of students (between 1 and 3) studies a software project and presents it to the audience with slides: the licences used by a scientific project, its economic model, the type of application and any other aspect of the software, and its level of reproducibility — whether the sources match the pseudo-codes of the article, and the findings for or against its reproducibility. Grading: the final presentation of the project 80 %, the intermediate TP presentations 20 % (master-mva.com) · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (continuous assessment that is not the whole grade)
  Prerequisites        not displayed
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who already writes research code in Python, has met git, and will soon publish, reuse or review code, articles and data.

**Empirical first**: sum the same 100,000 single-precision numbers from left to right and from right to left, and you get −423.29346 and −423.29407 (code in ch. 6). Copy a function from a public repository that has no licence file, and by default you have no right to redistribute it (ch. 1). Report the best of ten training seeds, and you announce a gain of about 1.5 standard deviations that does not exist (ch. 5). This course explains these numerical, legal and statistical failures and how a reproducible publication avoids them.

The course has two halves. The first studies free software as a legal and economic object: what a licence grants, how licences combine, and who pays for the software that research depends on. The second studies reproducible research: why published computational results often cannot be regenerated, and how to write, package, publish and review an article so that they can.

Related MVA pages: the practical follow-up [Open Science in the Age of AI: Reproducible Research Project](../s2-reproducible-research-project/index.html), the legal frame of [Regulating AI](../s2-regulating-ai/index.html), and the reproducible IPOL experiments used in [Image Denoising](../s1-image-denoising/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Distinguish free software, open source, source-available and proprietary software, and state the four freedoms and the criteria of the Open Source Definition.
-   Read a licence: identify its permissions, conditions and limitations, the scope of its copyleft and its patent clauses.
-   Decide whether components under different licences can be combined and distributed, and write the SPDX expression of the result.
-   Analyse the economic model of a free software project, and explain its under-provision with the volunteer's dilemma.
-   Evaluate a software project with a fixed grid: type of application, licences, rights holders, governance, economic model and reproducibility.
-   Define reproducibility, replicability and robustness, and quantify how low power, multiple testing and seed picking produce irreproducible claims.
-   Control the numerical sources of irreproducibility: summation order, floating-point tolerances, pseudo-random seeds and streams.
-   Freeze and record a software environment, read version control as a tamper-evident history, and build a pipeline that recomputes exactly what changed.
-   Describe the editorial process of journals and conferences, and of venues that review code, such as IPOL and ReScience C.
-   Identify who owns the code, the article and the data of a research project, and which terms make a reproducibility package redistributable.
-   Write an article whose pseudo-code, code, figures and numbers can be checked against each other, and audit somebody else's.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents a course on free software and reproducible research: how to write and publish reproducible research, the legal aspects of the code, the article and the data, and the good practices to write free software and perform reproducible research. Group discussions, debates and individual dissertations are part of the activities.

The description states that the plan covers the minimum knowledge that any PhD candidate or master's student in computational sciences should reach to perform reliable research. ### Course outline

-   **Review: floating point, probability and graphs** — the rounding model, Bayes' formula and tests, directed acyclic graphs and hash functions.
-   **Free and open-source software: introduction** — software as a copyrighted work, the four freedoms, the Open Source Definition, a short history.
-   **Licensing** — permissions, conditions and copyleft; when licences can be combined; SPDX; French and European licences; patents.
-   **Economic models of free software projects** — software as a public good, the volunteer's dilemma, business models, relicensing and forks, the truck factor.
-   **Case studies** — an analysis grid applied to the Linux kernel, scikit-learn, OpenCV and dual-licensed projects.
-   **Reproducible research: introduction** — vocabulary, evidence of a crisis, sources of irreproducibility, and the statistics of findings that do not replicate.
-   **Numerical determinism** — rounding errors in sums, compensated summation, sources of nondeterminism, pseudo-random generators and seeds.
-   **Software environments, version control and provenance** — dependency resolution, git as a Merkle graph, content-addressed pipelines.
-   **Publishing reproducible research: the editorial process** — the journey of a manuscript, the noise of peer review, venues that review code, identifiers and archives.
-   **Legal aspects of the code, the article and the data** — ownership, open access, database rights and personal data, redistributable packages, model weights.
-   **Writing a reproducible scientific article** — matching pseudo-code and code, tests with tolerances, reporting over seeds, packaging, auditing.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — long-term reproducibility, reproducible arithmetic, variance in benchmarks, automated reproduction, sustainability (self-study).

### How to study this module {#study}

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session: it reviews the M1 tools used later. Then read the chapters in order, each using only earlier ones; ch. 2 is used by ch. 4 and 9, ch. 6 by ch. 10 and 11, and ch. 7 by ch. 10.
-   Choose the software project of your group before session 4, and fill one line of the grid of Definition 4.1 after each lecture.
-   After each session, do the exercises of its row; the ★ ones check the definitions, the ★★ ones ask for a short proof or a computation.
-   Run every Python block. They use only the standard library, NumPy, SciPy and, in Ex. 8, NetworkX; each runs on a laptop in a few seconds, with fixed seeds.
-   Keep a lab notebook from the first day: the commit hash, the environment and the seed of every result you show in a partial presentation.
-   These notes are not legal advice. Each statement of law names its source; for a real decision, ask your institution's legal or technology-transfer office.

## 0. Review: floating point, probability and graphs {#ch0}

Three M1 tools return throughout the course: the rounding model of floating-point arithmetic (ch. 6 and 10), Bayes' formula with the vocabulary of tests (ch. 5 and 8), and directed acyclic graphs with hash functions (ch. 7). This chapter states them in the form used later.

### 0.1 Floating-point numbers

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Binary floating-point numbers]{.tag} A binary floating-point format of precision $p$ represents the non-zero numbers
$$
x = \pm\, m \times 2^{e-p+1}, \qquad m \in \mathbb{N}, \quad 2^{p-1} \le m < 2^{p},
$$
with an exponent $e$ in a bounded range, so that $2^e \le |x| < 2^{e+1}$. IEEE 754 binary64 (`float64`) has $p = 53$; binary32 (`float32`) has $p = 24$.

The **unit roundoff** of the format is
$$
u = 2^{-p}, \qquad u_{64} \approx 1.11 \times 10^{-16}, \qquad u_{32} \approx 5.96 \times 10^{-8}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — The standard model of rounding]{.tag} With rounding to nearest, and without overflow or underflow, each operation $\circ \in \{+, -, \times, /\}$ satisfies
$$
\mathrm{fl}(x \circ y) = (x \circ y)(1 + \delta), \qquad |\delta| \le u .
$$

::: proof
IEEE 754 requires the computed result to be the exact result, correctly rounded. Let $z = x \circ y \neq 0$ with $2^e \le |z| < 2^{e+1}$.

In that range, consecutive floating-point numbers are $2^{e-p+1}$ apart, so the nearest one is at distance at most half of that:
$$
|\mathrm{fl}(z) - z| \le 2^{e-p} \le 2^{-p}\,|z| = u\,|z| .
$$

Setting $\delta = (\mathrm{fl}(z) - z)/z$ gives the claim. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Each operation is accurate, but associativity is lost: a sum depends on the order of its terms. Near $10^{16}$, binary64 numbers are 2 apart, so adding 1 to $10^{16}$ does nothing.

```python
import numpy as np

u = np.finfo(np.float64).eps / 2          # unit roundoff of binary64
print(f"u = {u:.3e}")                      # 1.110e-16
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, repr(0.1 + 0.2))   # False 0.30000000000000004
print((1e16 + 1.0) - 1e16, (1e16 - 1e16) + 1.0)  # 0.0 1.0
print(np.spacing(1e16))                    # gap between neighbours of 1e16: 2.0
```

### 0.2 Bayes' formula and tests

For events $A$ and $B$ with $\mathbb{P}(B) > 0$, Bayes' formula with the law of total probability reads
$$
\mathbb{P}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(B \mid A)\,\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B \mid A)\,\mathbb{P}(A) + \mathbb{P}(B \mid A^c)\,\mathbb{P}(A^c)} .
$$

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Level, power and p-value]{.tag} A test at level $\alpha$ rejects a true null hypothesis with probability at most $\alpha$ (type I error). Its **power** $1 - \beta$ is the probability of rejecting under a given alternative; $\beta$ is the type II error.

For a statistic that is $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ under the null hypothesis, the two-sided p-value of an observed value $z$ is
$$
p = 2\,\big(1 - \Phi(|z|)\big),
$$
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. Write $z_q = \Phi^{-1}(q)$ for its quantiles. Thus $p \le 0.05$ exactly when $|z| \ge z_{0.975} \approx 1.96$.
:::

### 0.3 Directed acyclic graphs and hash functions

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — DAG and topological order]{.tag} A directed graph $G = (V, E)$ is **acyclic** (a DAG) if it has no directed cycle. A **topological order** is a bijective numbering $\pi : V \to \{1, \dots, |V|\}$ such that every edge goes forward:
$$
(u, v) \in E \implies \pi(u) < \pi(v).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Topological orders exist exactly on DAGs]{.tag} A finite directed graph has a topological order if and only if it is acyclic.

::: proof
On a cycle $v_1 \to \dots \to v_k \to v_1$, an order would need $\pi(v_1) < \dots < \pi(v_k) < \pi(v_1)$, which is impossible.

Conversely, a finite DAG has a vertex without incoming edge: otherwise, walking backwards along incoming edges would revisit a vertex and close a cycle. Number that vertex 1, delete it, and conclude by induction on $|V|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Hash function, collision]{.tag} A hash function maps strings of any length to strings of fixed length,
$$
H : \{0, 1\}^* \to \{0, 1\}^k ,
$$
with $k = 160$ for SHA-1 and $k = 256$ for SHA-256. A **collision** is a pair $x \neq x'$ with $H(x) = H(x')$. Collisions exist by the pigeonhole principle; $H$ is **collision resistant** when no feasible computation is known to find one.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — Birthday bound]{.tag} If $q$ inputs receive independent uniform hash values in $\{0, 1\}^k$, the probability that two of them collide is at most
$$
\frac{q(q-1)}{2^{k+1}} \le \frac{q^2}{2^{k+1}} .
$$

::: proof
There are $q(q-1)/2$ pairs, and each pair collides with probability $2^{-k}$; the union bound concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::

With $q = 10^9$ files and $k = 160$, the bound is about $3 \times 10^{-31}$: accidental collisions do not happen. Deliberate ones are discussed in ch. 7.
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Each floating-point operation has a relative error at most $u$, but sums depend on the order of their terms.
-   Bayes' formula turns the level and power of a test into the probability that a finding is true (ch. 5).
-   A finite directed graph has a topological order exactly when it is acyclic.
-   A collision-resistant hash gives a short, practically unique name to any file.
:::

## 1. Free and open-source software: introduction {#ch1}

This chapter fixes the vocabulary of the course: what software is as a legal object, who controls it by default, and what “free software” and “open source” promise.

### 1.1 Source code and copyright

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Source code and object code]{.tag} The GNU GPL version 3 (section 1) defines the **source code** of a work as “the preferred form of the work for making modifications to it”. **Object code** is any other form, such as a compiled binary. For a trained model, which form is preferred for modification (weights, training code, data) is debated (ch. 9.6).
:::

A computer program is protected by copyright as a literary work: under the Berne Convention as applied by the TRIPS agreement (article 10), the European Directive 2009/24/EC, and, in France, article L112-2 of the Code de la propriété intellectuelle.

Protection is automatic, without registration, and lasts in the European Union until 70 years after the author's death. It covers the expression, that is the code, but not the ideas and principles behind it (Directive 2009/24/EC, article 1(2)), which include algorithms insofar as they are ideas.

::: key
[Default rule]{.tag} Without a licence, all rights are reserved. Reading code on a public web page gives no right to copy, modify or redistribute it.
:::

The rights holder is the author or, for software written by an employee in the course of their duties, the employer (ch. 9.2). A **licence** is the document by which the rights holder grants others some of these rights.

### 1.2 Free software and open source

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Free software]{.tag} The Free Software Foundation (FSF) calls a program **free software** when its users have four freedoms:

-   freedom 0, to run the program as they wish, for any purpose;
-   freedom 1, to study how the program works and change it, which requires the source code;
-   freedom 2, to redistribute copies;
-   freedom 3, to distribute copies of modified versions.

“Free” refers to liberty, not price: free software may be sold.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Open source]{.tag} The Open Source Initiative (OSI) approves a licence as **open source** when it meets the ten criteria of the Open Source Definition: free redistribution; source code; derived works allowed; integrity of the author's source code; no discrimination against persons or groups; no discrimination against fields of endeavour; distribution of the licence; licence not specific to a product; licence not restricting other software; licence technology-neutral.
:::

The two definitions come from different philosophies, ethical for the FSF and practical for the OSI, but select almost the same licences, hence the umbrella term FOSS. Exceptions are rare: the OSI approves the NASA Open Source Agreement 1.3, which the FSF does not consider free.

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Neighbouring categories]{.tag} **Freeware** costs nothing but gives neither source nor freedoms. **Source-available** software shows its source but withholds a freedom, such as commercial use or hosting. A **public domain dedication** waives all rights as far as the law allows; CC0 adds a fallback licence. Everything else is **proprietary**.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — Free or not?]{.tag}

-   CC BY-NC 4.0 forbids commercial use, a field of endeavour: neither free nor open source.
-   The JSON licence adds to an MIT text “The Software shall be used for Good, not Evil”; this restriction on use breaks freedom 0, so the FSF does not consider it free, and the OSI has not approved it.
-   The Business Source License 1.1 restricts production use until a change date, at most four years after each release, when the code switches to an open licence: source-available.
-   The MIT licence only asks to keep the copyright and permission notice: free and open source.
:::

### 1.3 A short history

-   **1983–1989**: Richard Stallman announces the GNU project, creates the FSF (1985) and publishes the GNU General Public License (1989).
-   **1991–1992**: Linus Torvalds releases Linux (1991) and places it under the GPL version 2 the following year.
-   **1998**: the term “open source” is adopted and the OSI founded, after Netscape announces the release of its browser's source code.
-   **2001–2007**: Creative Commons is founded (2001) to license texts and images; the GPL version 3 appears (2007).

### 1.4 Why free software matters for research

A computational result can be checked only if its code can be run for any purpose, read and passed to a colleague: freedoms 0, 1 and 2. A proprietary dependency or a discontinued version can make a result impossible to regenerate. A free licence is necessary but not sufficient: the code must also be available, documented, runnable and faithful to the article, the subject of ch. 5–10.

::: note
[Debate]{.tag} Is code released on a public platform without a licence “open”? Should the code of a thesis be released before the defence, and under whose name? Prepare one argument for each side, using ch. 1.1 and ch. 9.2.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   Software is protected by copyright automatically; without a licence, nothing may be redistributed.
-   Free software guarantees four freedoms; open source is defined by ten criteria; both select nearly the same licences.
-   Restrictions on commercial use or on fields of use make a licence non-free.
-   Reproducibility needs free software, but also availability, documentation and faithfulness to the article.
:::

## 2. Licensing {#ch2}

A licence turns the default “all rights reserved” into a list of what others may do. This chapter reads licences clause by clause, sorts them into families, and answers the question every project meets: can these components be distributed together?

### 2.1 Anatomy of a licence

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Permissions, conditions, limitations]{.tag} A free software licence is a permission granted by the rights holder to anyone who accepts its terms. Its clauses are of three kinds:

-   **permissions**: use, copy, modify, distribute, sublicense, sometimes use the contributors' patents;
-   **conditions**: keep the notices, state the changes, provide the source, keep the same licence;
-   **limitations**: no warranty, no liability, no trademark rights.

If a condition is not met, the permission lapses and further use infringes copyright; the GPL version 3 (section 8) lets the violation be cured.
:::

### 2.2 Families and copyleft

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Copyleft]{.tag} A **copyleft** licence requires that distributed modified versions, and, depending on its *scope*, larger works containing the code, be licensed under the same terms, with their source. A **permissive** licence only asks to keep the notices: the code may enter a work under any licence, proprietary included.
:::

| Licence (SPDX identifier) | Family | Copyleft scope | Explicit patent grant |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MIT`, `BSD-3-Clause` | permissive | none | no |
| `Apache-2.0` (2004) | permissive | none | yes, ended for whoever sues over patents |
| `MPL-2.0` (2012) | weak copyleft | modified files | yes |
| `LGPL-2.1-only`, `LGPL-3.0-only` | weak copyleft | the library, not programs linking to it | in version 3 |
| `GPL-2.0-only` (1991) | strong copyleft | whole program | no |
| `GPL-3.0-only` (2007) | strong copyleft | whole program | yes |
| `AGPL-3.0-only` (2007) | network copyleft | whole program, also used over a network | yes |

Copyleft is triggered by **distribution**: private use and modification carry no obligation. Running a program as a network service is not distribution, so the GPL asks nothing of the operator; the AGPL (section 13) closes this gap by obliging the operator to offer the source to remote users. The GPL does not extend to a **mere aggregation** of separate programs; the FSF holds that linking a library creates a combined work, and the LGPL was written to allow linking from programs under other licences.

### 2.3 When can licences be combined?

The following model makes the question precise; it simplifies legal reasoning and does not replace it.

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Compatibility model]{.tag} Describe a licence $\ell$ by two sets of conditions on a distributed work that contains $\ell$-licensed code: the conditions $O(\ell)$ it imposes, and the conditions $A(\ell) \supseteq O(\ell)$ it tolerates. A permissive licence tolerates every condition; a copyleft licence only its own and those it explicitly allows.

Licences $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k$ are **compatible** if each tolerates all the imposed conditions:
$$
O := \bigcup_{i=1}^{k} O(\ell_i) \subseteq A(\ell_j) \quad \text{for every } j .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Compatibility is decided pair by pair]{.tag} In the model of Definition 2.3, a set of licences is compatible if and only if each pair of its licences is compatible.

::: proof
($\Rightarrow$) The conditions imposed by a pair satisfy
$$
O(\ell_i) \cup O(\ell_j) \subseteq O \subseteq A(\ell_i) \cap A(\ell_j).
$$

($\Leftarrow$) Pairwise compatibility gives $O(\ell_i) \subseteq A(\ell_j)$ for all $i \neq j$, and $O(\ell_j) \subseteq A(\ell_j)$ holds by definition.

Taking the union over $i$ gives $O \subseteq A(\ell_j)$ for every $j$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Compatibility is not transitive: MIT code is compatible with Apache-2.0 and with the GPL version 2, but, according to the FSF, Apache-2.0 is not compatible with the GPL version 2, whose ban on further restrictions excludes Apache's patent termination clause. Compatible sets are the cliques of the compatibility graph.
::::

The code encodes facts from the FSF's licence list: MIT and BSD-3-Clause are compatible with both GPL versions; Apache-2.0 only with version 3; `GPL-2.0-only` and version 3 are incompatible, but “version 2 or later” code can be used under version 3; the GPL and AGPL version 3 allow combination (section 13 of both).

```python
# Toy model of Definition 2.3: a licence = (imposed conditions O, tolerated conditions A).
ANY = None  # permissive: tolerates any condition on the combined work
GPL3_OK = {"notice", "no-endorsement", "state-changes", "patent-termination",
           "source", "under-GPL-3.0", "network-source"}
LIC = {
    "MIT":              ({"notice"}, ANY),
    "BSD-3-Clause":     ({"notice", "no-endorsement"}, ANY),
    "Apache-2.0":       ({"notice", "state-changes", "patent-termination"}, ANY),
    "GPL-2.0-only":     ({"notice", "source", "under-GPL-2.0"},
                         {"notice", "no-endorsement", "source", "under-GPL-2.0"}),
    "GPL-3.0-or-later": ({"notice", "source", "under-GPL-3.0"}, GPL3_OK),
    "AGPL-3.0-only":    ({"notice", "source", "under-GPL-3.0", "network-source"}, GPL3_OK),
}

def compatible(licences):
    O = set().union(*(LIC[l][0] for l in licences))
    return all(LIC[l][1] is ANY or O <= LIC[l][1] for l in licences)

names = list(LIC)
print([(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(names) for b in names[i + 1:] if not compatible([a, b])])
print(compatible(["MIT", "Apache-2.0", "GPL-3.0-or-later"]))   # True
print(compatible(["MIT", "Apache-2.0", "GPL-2.0-only"]))       # False

def spdx_ok(expr, accepted):
    """Evaluate an SPDX expression without parentheses: AND binds tighter than OR."""
    return any(all(t.strip() in accepted for t in conj.split(" AND "))
               for conj in expr.split(" OR "))

print(spdx_ok("MIT OR Apache-2.0", {"Apache-2.0"}))                 # True
print(spdx_ok("GPL-2.0-only AND BSD-3-Clause", {"BSD-3-Clause"}))   # False
```

The model finds three incompatible pairs: Apache-2.0 with `GPL-2.0-only`, and `GPL-2.0-only` with each version-3 licence.

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — A thesis repository]{.tag} A repository combines the student's code, an MIT plotting helper, an Apache-2.0 data loader and a function copied from a `GPL-2.0-only` project. By Proposition 2.4 it is incompatible, because of the pair Apache-2.0 and `GPL-2.0-only`. Fixes: rewrite the function; call the GPL program as a separate executable (aggregation); or obtain “version 2 or later” and distribute everything under `GPL-3.0-or-later`.
:::

The model ignores the kind of combination (copying, linking, separate processes), licence exceptions, and the fact that only courts settle interpretations. These notes are not legal advice.

### 2.4 Applying a licence: SPDX and REUSE

**SPDX**, a Linux Foundation project standardised as ISO/IEC 5962:2021, names every licence and combines names into expressions, which `spdx_ok` above evaluates:

-   `MIT OR Apache-2.0`: the recipient chooses either licence;
-   `GPL-2.0-only AND BSD-3-Clause`: both apply, for instance to two parts of a package;
-   `GPL-2.0-only WITH Linux-syscall-note`: a licence with an additional permission.

To license a project, put the licence text in a `LICENSE` file, start each source file with a copyright line and `SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-or-later`, declare the expression in the package metadata (`License-Expression` for Python), and check the tree with the REUSE tool of the Free Software Foundation Europe.

### 2.5 French and European licences

-   **CeCILL** (CEA, CNRS, Inria), in French and English, governed by French law: CeCILL-2.1 (2013) is a copyleft that explicitly allows relicensing under the GNU GPL; CeCILL-B is permissive with a strong citation obligation; CeCILL-C is a library-level copyleft, close to the LGPL.
-   **EUPL-1.2** (European Commission, 2017), a copyleft in the official languages of the European Union, whose appendix lists compatible licences, among them the GPL, AGPL, LGPL, MPL-2.0 and CeCILL-2.x.

### 2.6 Patents

Copyright protects the code; a **patent** protects an invention, possibly the method the code implements, whoever wrote it. A free licence does not guarantee freedom to use a method patented by a third party. The European Patent Convention (article 52) excludes programs for computers “as such”, but software-related inventions with a technical character can be patented in Europe.

::: ex
[Example 2.6 — The SIFT patent]{.tag} Lowe's SIFT detector was covered by United States patent 6,711,293, held by the University of British Columbia. OpenCV kept it in a separate “non-free” module until the patent expired in March 2020; SIFT then joined the main library in release 4.4.0. Patent grants such as Apache-2.0's would not have helped: they cover only the contributors' own patents.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   A licence grants permissions under conditions; breaking a condition ends the permission.
-   Copyleft scope ranges from none to the file, the library, the program and network use.
-   In the model of Definition 2.3, compatibility is decided pair by pair but is not transitive.
-   Declare licences with SPDX expressions, a `LICENSE` file and per-file headers.
-   Patents are a separate layer from copyright licences.
:::

## 3. Economic models of free software projects {#ch3}

Free software costs nothing to copy, yet years of work to write and maintain. This chapter explains why such a good is under-provided, how projects finance themselves, and how to measure their fragility.

### 3.1 Software as a public good

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Rivalry, excludability, public good]{.tag} A good is **rival** when one person's use prevents another's, and **excludable** when its owner can prevent use by those who do not pay. A **public good** is neither; Samuelson (1954) formalised the non-rival case.
:::

Copying software costs almost nothing, and a free licence gives up the right to exclude: free software is a public good. Its private provision is then insufficient, since each user prefers that another one pays (Bergstrom, Blume and Varian, 1986). The volunteer's dilemma quantifies this.

### 3.2 The volunteer's dilemma

Consider $n \ge 2$ users of a library. If at least one of them fixes a critical bug, each gains $v > 0$; fixing costs the volunteer $c$, with $0 < c < v$.

The payoffs are:

-   $v - c$ for a volunteer;
-   $v$ for an abstainer when someone volunteers;
-   $0$ for everyone when nobody does.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Volunteer's dilemma (Diekmann, 1985)]{.tag}

-   (a) The pure Nash equilibria are the $n$ profiles in which exactly one user volunteers.
-   (b) There is a unique symmetric equilibrium. In it, each user abstains with probability
$$
q = (c/v)^{1/(n-1)} .
$$
-   (c) In that equilibrium, the probability that nobody volunteers is
$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{nobody}) = (c/v)^{n/(n-1)},
$$
which increases with $n$ and tends to $c/v$.

::: proof
(a) If nobody volunteers, anyone gains $v - c > 0$ by volunteering. If two or more volunteer, one of them gains $c$ by abstaining. If exactly one volunteers, they would lose $v - c$ by abstaining, and the others already get the maximum $v$.

(b) By (a), no symmetric pure profile is an equilibrium, so $0 < q < 1$ and each user is indifferent between the two actions. Volunteering yields $v - c$; abstaining yields $v$ unless the $n - 1$ others all abstain:
$$
v - c = v\,\big(1 - q^{n-1}\big) \iff q^{n-1} = c/v .
$$

(c) Nobody volunteers with probability $q^n = (c/v)^{n/(n-1)}$; as $0 < c/v < 1$ and the exponent decreases to 1, this increases to $c/v$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — More users, less maintenance]{.tag} With $v = 10$ and $c = 4$:

| Users $n$ | Abstention probability $q$ | $\mathbb{P}(\text{nobody})$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.400 | 0.160 |
| 5 | 0.795 | 0.318 |
| 10 | 0.903 | 0.361 |
| 100 | 0.991 | 0.396 |

From 2 to 100 users, the risk that the bug is never fixed more than doubles.
:::

The pure equilibria show the remedy: coordination that designates the volunteer, as maintainers paid by a company, a foundation or a research institute do.

### 3.3 Why people contribute

Lerner and Tirole (2002) distinguish immediate benefits, such as needing the fix oneself (the “itch” of Raymond, 1999) or being paid for it, from delayed ones: public contributions signal skill to future employers and peers. In research, code is part of the output, but the credit it receives remains weak compared with articles (ch. 8.4).

### 3.4 Business models

| Model | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Support and subscriptions | certified builds, updates, support | Red Hat Enterprise Linux |
| Dual licensing | copyleft for all, a paid licence for proprietary use | MySQL, Qt, CGAL |
| Open core | free core, proprietary extensions | GitLab |
| Hosting | sell the running service | managed databases |
| Foundations | member fees, neutral governance | Linux Foundation, Apache Software Foundation, NumFOCUS |
| Grants and donations | public or philanthropic money, sponsorship | Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Sovereign Tech Fund, GitHub Sponsors |
| Research institutions | salaried researchers and engineers | Inria, CNRS, universities |

Dual licensing needs one entity able to sell a licence for the whole code, hence **contributor licence agreements** (CLAs) that grant it the necessary rights.

### 3.5 Relicensing and forks

::: note
[Rule — What a relicensing can and cannot do]{.tag} A project can change the licence of its future versions alone only if it holds the rights on every contribution, directly or through CLAs. Free licences are generally irrevocable (GPL version 3, section 2; Apache-2.0, section 2), so released versions stay under their licence, and anyone may **fork** the last of them, that is, continue it independently.
:::

Three recent cases follow one pattern: cloud competition, a move to a source-available licence, a community fork.

-   **Elasticsearch** left Apache-2.0 in 2021; the OpenSearch fork kept it. Elastic added the AGPL version 3 as an option in 2024.
-   **Terraform** moved from MPL-2.0 to the Business Source License in 2023; the OpenTofu fork is hosted by the Linux Foundation.
-   **Redis** left BSD-3-Clause in 2024; the Valkey fork is hosted by the Linux Foundation. Redis added the AGPL version 3 as an option in 2025.

### 3.6 Measuring fragility: the truck factor

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Truck factor (Avelino et al., 2016)]{.tag} Let $F$ be the files of a project and $D$ its developers, file $f$ having authors $a(f) \subseteq D$. A file is **orphaned** by the departure of $S \subseteq D$ when $a(f) \subseteq S$. The **truck factor** is the smallest number of departures that orphan more than half of the files:
$$
\mathrm{TF} = \min \big\{ |S| : |\{ f \in F : a(f) \subseteq S \}| > |F|/2 \big\} .
$$
:::

Avelino and coauthors estimate it greedily, removing at each step the developer who authors the most files. The code uses a variant that removes the developer whose departure orphans the most files, compares it with exhaustive search, and checks Theorem 3.2 by simulation.

```python
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

# Volunteer's dilemma (Theorem 3.2): value v, cost c, n users
v, c = 10.0, 4.0
for n in [2, 5, 10, 100]:
    q = (c / v) ** (1 / (n - 1))          # probability of abstaining
    print(f"n={n:3d}  q={q:.3f}  P(nobody)={q**n:.3f}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 10; q = (c / v) ** (1 / (n - 1))
print("simulated, n=10:", (rng.random((200_000, n)) < q).all(axis=1).mean())

# Truck factor (Definition 3.4) on a synthetic authorship relation
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n_files, n_dev = 60, 8
p = 1 / np.arange(1, n_dev + 1); p /= p.sum()          # a few prolific authors
authors = [set(rng.choice(n_dev, size=rng.integers(1, 3), replace=False, p=p))
           for _ in range(n_files)]
orphaned = lambda S: sum(a <= S for a in authors)

def truck_factor_greedy():
    S = set()
    while orphaned(S) <= n_files / 2:
        S.add(max(set(range(n_dev)) - S, key=lambda d: orphaned(S | {d})))
    return len(S)

def truck_factor_exact():
    return next(k for k in range(1, n_dev + 1)
                if any(orphaned(set(S)) > n_files / 2 for S in combinations(range(n_dev), k)))

print("greedy:", truck_factor_greedy(), " exact:", truck_factor_exact())   # 3 and 3
```

Both give 3 here, but a greedy heuristic can overestimate the truck factor (Ex. 9).

::: note
[Debate]{.tag} A laboratory publishes a library used by thousands of researchers. Must it maintain it, and who should pay: the laboratory, its funders, or the users' institutions? Use Theorem 3.2 and ch. 3.4.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Free software is a public good, hence privately under-provided.
-   In the symmetric volunteer's dilemma, the risk that nobody does the work grows with the number of users.
-   Projects live on support, dual licensing, open core, hosting, foundations, grants and research institutions.
-   Released versions keep their licence; relicensing needs all the rights and often triggers a fork.
-   The truck factor counts the departures that would orphan most of the code.
:::

## 4. Case studies {#ch4}

The official assessment asks each group to study a real software project. This chapter fixes a grid for that study and applies it to a kernel with thousands of rights holders, a scientific library, a computer-vision library hit by a patent, and dual-licensed products.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Analysis grid of a software project]{.tag} This page proposes seven lines, following the official assessment:

1.  **Type of application**: library, application, service or framework; domain; users.
2.  **Licences**: main licence, SPDX expression of the distribution, licences of dependencies and vendored code, compatibility (ch. 2).
3.  **Rights holders**: individuals, institutions or one company; CLA or Developer Certificate of Origin.
4.  **Governance**: maintainer, company, steering council or foundation.
5.  **Economic model**: rows of the table of ch. 3.4.
6.  **Community health**: active contributors, truck factor, release cadence.
7.  **Reproducibility**: archived releases, tests, an associated article, agreement between its pseudo-code and the code (ch. 10).
:::

### 4.1 The Linux kernel

-   **Licence**: `GPL-2.0-only`, with a note excluding from the copyleft the user programs that only use system calls (`GPL-2.0-only WITH Linux-syscall-note`).
-   **Rights holders**: thousands of contributors keep their copyright, without CLA; each patch certifies the Developer Certificate of Origin (2004) by a “Signed-off-by” line. A move to the GPL version 3 would need all their consents (ch. 3.5): practically impossible.
-   **Economic model**: most changes are written by developers employed by companies; the Linux Foundation provides neutral governance.

### 4.2 scikit-learn

-   **Type and licence**: a Python machine-learning library under `BSD-3-Clause`, started as a Google Summer of Code project (2007) and first released publicly by Inria researchers in 2010; Pedregosa et al. (2011) is its reference article.
-   **Economic model**: the permissive licence lets companies embed it in proprietary products, which brings users and sponsors; a consortium hosted by the Inria Foundation has funded maintainers since 2018.
-   **Reproducibility**: the `random_state` parameter of randomised estimators, deprecation cycles, extensive tests, documentation for each version.

### 4.3 OpenCV and the SIFT patent

-   **Licence**: `BSD-3-Clause` until release 4.4, `Apache-2.0` from release 4.5.0 (2020), which adds a patent grant from contributors.
-   **Patents**: SIFT and SURF lived in a non-free module enabled at build time (Example 2.6).
-   **Lesson**: the copyright licence, third-party patents and the build options that select what is distributed are three layers to check separately.

### 4.4 Dual licensing: MySQL, Qt and CGAL

-   **MySQL**: the GPL version 2 or a commercial licence. When Oracle announced in 2009 the acquisition of Sun, owner of MySQL, the original author of MySQL started the MariaDB fork.
-   **Qt**: the GPL, the LGPL version 3, or commercial licences sold by The Qt Company.
-   **CGAL**, the Computational Geometry Algorithms Library: most packages under `GPL-3.0-or-later`, the kernel under `LGPL-3.0-or-later`, commercial licences sold by GeometryFactory. Academic users get free software; industrial users pay.

### 4.5 A licence inventory of your own environment

The grid starts with an inventory. Python packages declare their licence in their metadata, as an SPDX expression or, in older packages, as a classifier or free text.

```python
from collections import Counter
from importlib import metadata

def licence_of(dist):
    """Best-effort licence string from package metadata (SPDX expression first)."""
    m = dist.metadata
    if m.get("License-Expression"):
        return m["License-Expression"]
    classifiers = [c.split(" :: ")[-1] for c in (m.get_all("Classifier") or [])
                   if c.startswith("License ::")]
    if classifiers:
        return classifiers[0]
    text = (m.get("License") or "").strip().splitlines()
    return text[0][:40] if text else "UNKNOWN"

for name in ["numpy", "scipy", "scikit-learn", "networkx"]:
    try:
        d = metadata.distribution(name)
        print(f"{name:13s} {d.version:10s} {licence_of(d)}")
    except metadata.PackageNotFoundError:
        print(f"{name:13s} not installed")

print(Counter(licence_of(d) for d in metadata.distributions()).most_common(5))
```

A “BSD” project is often an AND of licences: the NumPy release used to test these notes (2.5.3) declares `BSD-3-Clause AND 0BSD AND MIT AND Zlib AND CC0-1.0`, one licence per vendored component. A free-text “BSD License” does not say which BSD licence applies; then read the `LICENSE` file itself.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   The grid of Definition 4.1 covers type, licences, rights holders, governance, economic model, community and reproducibility.
-   Without a CLA, a project with many rights holders cannot change its licence.
-   A permissive licence attracts industrial users; dual licensing needs a single rights holder.
-   Copyright licences, patents and build options are separate layers.
:::

## 5. Reproducible research: introduction {#ch5}

A computational article makes claims that depend on code, data and an environment that the reader rarely sees. This chapter defines what reproducing such a claim means, reviews the evidence that many claims cannot be reproduced, and quantifies the statistical side of the problem.

### 5.1 Origins and vocabulary

In the early 1990s, Jon Claerbout's group at Stanford arranged its books and theses so that every figure could be rebuilt by one command (Claerbout and Karrenbach, 1992). Buckheit and Donoho (1995) summarised the idea:

> An article about computational science in a scientific publication is not the scholarship itself, it is merely advertising of the scholarship. The actual scholarship is the complete software development environment and the complete set of instructions which generated the figures.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Reproducibility and replicability (National Academies, 2019)]{.tag}

-   **Reproducibility**: obtaining consistent computational results using the same input data, computational steps, methods, code and conditions of analysis.
-   **Replicability**: obtaining consistent results across studies aimed at answering the same scientific question, each of which has obtained its own data.

The Turing Way adds: a result is **robust** when a different analysis of the same data gives it, and **generalisable** when it survives new data and a new analysis.
:::

Some communities swap the two words (Barba, 2018; Plesser, 2018); the ACM swapped the meanings of its badges in 2020 to align with the definitions above. Always state yours. Peng (2011) describes a spectrum: publication only; with code; with code and data; with linked, executable code and data; full replication.

### 5.2 Evidence

-   **Psychology**: the Open Science Collaboration (2015) repeated 100 studies; 97 % of the originals had significant results, against 36 % of the replications.
-   **All sciences**: among 1,576 researchers surveyed by *Nature* (Baker, 2016), more than 70 % had failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments.
-   **Machine learning**: Raff (2019) attempted to reimplement 255 papers without their code and succeeded for about 63.5 %; Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) traced many failures to data leakage.
-   **Notebooks**: of about 1.4 million Jupyter notebooks collected by Pimentel et al. (2019), about a quarter of those re-executed ran without error, and about 4 % reproduced their stored results.

### 5.3 Sources of irreproducibility

| Source | Example | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Missing artefacts | code “on request” | licence and archive (ch. 2, 8) |
| Environment drift | a default value changes | lock the environment (ch. 7) |
| Numerical nondeterminism | parallel sums | tolerances, deterministic modes (ch. 6) |
| Unrecorded randomness | seed not reported | seed streams (ch. 6) |
| Article–code mismatch | pseudo-code differs from code | audit (ch. 10) |
| Analysis flexibility | best of many runs reported | statistics (ch. 5.4) |
| Data leakage | test data used in preprocessing | test set fixed in advance |
| Legal barriers | data not redistributable | terms of use (ch. 9) |

### 5.4 The statistics of findings that do not replicate

A perfectly reproducible computation can still support a claim that does not replicate.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Positive predictive value of a finding (Ioannidis, 2005)]{.tag} Among the hypotheses tested in a field, let $R$ be the ratio of true to false ones, tested at level $\alpha$ with power $1 - \beta$. The probability that a significant finding is true is
$$
\mathrm{PPV} = \frac{(1 - \beta)\,R}{(1 - \beta)\,R + \alpha} .
$$

::: proof
A tested hypothesis is true with probability $R/(1+R)$. Bayes' formula (ch. 0.2), with $A$ = “true” and $B$ = “significant”, gives
$$
\mathrm{PPV} = \frac{(1-\beta)\,\frac{R}{1+R}}{(1-\beta)\,\frac{R}{1+R} + \alpha\,\frac{1}{1+R}} ,
$$
and the factor $1/(1+R)$ cancels. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — Exploratory fields]{.tag} With $\alpha = 0.05$ and $R = 0.1$, the PPV is $0.08 / 0.13 \approx 0.615$ at power 0.8, and $0.02 / 0.07 \approx 0.286$ at power 0.2: in an underpowered field, most significant findings are false, without any error in the code.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Replicating a just-significant result (Goodman, 1992)]{.tag} A study observes a standardised statistic $z_{\mathrm{obs}} > 0$. If the true effect equals the observed one, a replication of the same size is significant at level $\alpha$, in the same direction, with probability
$$
\Phi\big(z_{\mathrm{obs}} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\big),
$$
which equals $1/2$ at $p = 0.05$ exactly.

::: proof
The replication statistic is then $Z' \sim \mathcal{N}(z_{\mathrm{obs}}, 1)$, significant in the same direction when $Z' > z_{1-\alpha/2}$, so with probability
$$
1 - \Phi\big(z_{1-\alpha/2} - z_{\mathrm{obs}}\big) = \Phi\big(z_{\mathrm{obs}} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\big).
$$
At $p = 0.05$, $z_{\mathrm{obs}} = z_{0.975}$ and $\Phi(0) = 1/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Multiple testing]{.tag} Among $m$ independent tests of true null hypotheses at level $\alpha$, at least one is significant with probability $1 - (1 - \alpha)^m$, about 0.64 for $m = 20$ and $\alpha = 0.05$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — The best of $n$ seeds]{.tag} If the scores of $n$ runs with different seeds are independent and $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\max_i X_i\big] = \mu + e_n\,\sigma, \qquad e_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \approx 0.564,\quad e_{10} \approx 1.539,
$$
and $e_n$ grows like $\sqrt{2 \ln n}$.

::: proof
For $n = 2$, write
$$
\max(X_1, X_2) = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{2} + \frac{|X_1 - X_2|}{2} .
$$

The difference $X_1 - X_2$ is $\mathcal{N}(0, 2\sigma^2)$, and $\mathbb{E}|Y| = s\sqrt{2/\pi}$ when $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, s^2)$, so the second term has mean $\sigma/\sqrt{\pi}$. The value of $e_{10}$ is computed below; the growth rate is the classical behaviour of Gaussian maxima. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Reporting the best of ten seeds inflates the result by about 1.5 standard deviations of the seed noise. Henderson et al. (2018) showed that, in deep reinforcement learning, averages over two small sets of seeds of the same algorithm can differ significantly.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

def ppv(R, power, alpha=0.05):                     # Theorem 5.2
    return power * R / (power * R + alpha)

for R in [1.0, 0.25, 0.1]:
    print(f"R={R:4.2f}  PPV(power .8)={ppv(R, .8):.3f}  PPV(power .2)={ppv(R, .2):.3f}")

z_crit = norm.ppf(0.975)                           # Proposition 5.4
for p in [0.05, 0.01, 0.005]:
    print(f"p={p:5.3f}  P(replication significant)={norm.cdf(norm.ppf(1 - p/2) - z_crit):.3f}")

print("P(at least one of 20 tests)", round(1 - 0.95**20, 3))   # Proposition 5.5

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                     # Proposition 5.6
for n in [2, 5, 10]:
    e_n = rng.standard_normal((100_000, n)).max(axis=1).mean()
    print(f"n={n:2d}  e_n = {e_n:.3f}")
```

::: note
[Debate]{.tag} A result can be reproduced only on its authors' private cluster, with proprietary data. Is it still a scientific result? What should a journal require: code, data, an executable environment, or an independent replication?
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Reproducibility reruns the same analysis on the same data; replicability obtains the result again with new data.
-   Psychology, surveys, machine learning and notebooks all show widespread failures.
-   Low prior odds and low power make most significant findings false (Theorem 5.2).
-   A just-significant result replicates half the time; the best of ten seeds overstates the mean by about $1.5\sigma$.
:::

## 6. Numerical determinism: floating point and pseudo-random numbers {#ch6}

Rerunning the same code on the same data does not guarantee the same numbers. This chapter bounds the effect of the order of floating-point operations, lists the sources of nondeterminism, and makes pseudo-random numbers reproducible.

### 6.1 Rounding errors in sums

For an integer $m$ with $mu < 1$, write
$$
\gamma_m = \frac{m u}{1 - m u} .
$$

:::: prop
[Lemma 6.1 — Products of rounding factors]{.tag} If $|\delta_k| \le u$ for $k = 1, \dots, m$ and $mu < 1$, then
$$
\Big|\prod_{k=1}^{m} (1 + \delta_k) - 1\Big| \le \gamma_m .
$$

::: proof
The product lies between $(1-u)^m$ and $(1+u)^m$. Above, $(1+u)^m \le e^{mu} \le 1/(1 - mu) = 1 + \gamma_m$, since $e^x \le 1/(1-x)$ for $0 \le x < 1$. Below, $(1-u)^m \ge 1 - mu \ge 1 - \gamma_m$ by Bernoulli's inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Error of recursive summation]{.tag} Let $s = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ and let $\hat s$ be computed from left to right in floating point, with $(n-1)u < 1$. Then
$$
|\hat s - s| \le \gamma_{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i| .
$$

::: proof
Let $\hat s_1 = x_1$ and $\hat s_k = (\hat s_{k-1} + x_k)(1 + \delta_k)$ for $k \ge 2$, with $|\delta_k| \le u$ by Proposition 0.2. Unrolling the recursion,
$$
\hat s = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \prod_{k=\max(i,2)}^{n} (1 + \delta_k) .
$$

Each product has at most $n - 1$ factors, hence differs from 1 by at most $\gamma_{n-1}$ (Lemma 6.1). Subtracting $s$ and using the triangle inequality concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Corollary 6.3 — Two orders, two results]{.tag} Any two summation orders, for instance those of two thread counts, give results within
$$
2\,\gamma_{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i|
$$
of each other, but generally not equal bit for bit: bitwise reproducibility requires a fixed order of operations.
:::

The bound is a worst case; rounding errors of random sign partly cancel (Ex. 11). **Compensated summation** carries the rounding error of each addition into the next.

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.4 — Kahan summation (Kahan, 1965)]{.tag}

1.  $s \leftarrow 0$, $c \leftarrow 0$.
2.  For $i = 1, \dots, n$: $y \leftarrow x_i - c$; $t \leftarrow s + y$; $c \leftarrow (t - s) - y$; $s \leftarrow t$.
3.  Return $s$.

Its error is at most $(2u + O(nu^2)) \sum_i |x_i|$, almost independent of $n$ (Higham, 2002, section 4.3).
:::

```python
import math
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
xs = rng.standard_normal(100_000).astype(np.float32)
ref = math.fsum(xs.astype(np.float64))            # correctly rounded reference

def naive(v):                                      # left-to-right summation
    s = np.float32(0)
    for t in v:
        s = np.float32(s + t)
    return s

def kahan(v):                                      # Algorithm 6.4
    s, c = np.float32(0), np.float32(0)
    for t in v:
        y = np.float32(t - c); t2 = np.float32(s + y)
        c = np.float32((t2 - s) - y); s = t2
    return s

u32 = np.finfo(np.float32).eps / 2
n = len(xs)
bound = (n - 1) * u32 / (1 - (n - 1) * u32) * np.abs(xs).astype(np.float64).sum()
for name, val in [("left to right", naive(xs)), ("right to left", naive(xs[::-1])),
                  ("numpy pairwise", xs.sum()), ("kahan", kahan(xs))]:
    print(f"{name:15s} {float(val):.5f}  error {abs(float(val) - ref):.1e}")
print(f"worst-case bound of Theorem 6.2: {bound:.1e}")
```

The order or rounding of operations also changes with the number of threads of a reduction or of a BLAS library, with atomic additions on GPUs, with compiler options such as `-ffast-math` or fused multiply–add, and with library versions. PyTorch's `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` raises an error when an operation has no deterministic implementation. Python also randomises string hashes in each process, so the iteration order of a set of strings may vary unless `PYTHONHASHSEED` is fixed.

### 6.2 Pseudo-random numbers

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Pseudo-random generator]{.tag} A pseudo-random generator is a finite state set $S$, a transition $f : S \to S$ and an output map $g$. A **seed** fixes the initial state $s_0$, then
$$
s_{k+1} = f(s_k), \qquad u_k = g(s_k) .
$$
As $S$ is finite, the states are eventually periodic; the **period** is the length of the cycle. The whole sequence is a deterministic function of the seed.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 6.6 — Full period of a linear congruential generator (Hull and Dobell, 1962)]{.tag} The generator $x_{k+1} = (a x_k + c) \bmod m$ has period $m$ for every seed if and only if:

-   $c$ and $m$ are coprime;
-   $a - 1$ is divisible by every prime factor of $m$;
-   $a - 1$ is divisible by 4 if $m$ is.

A proof is in Knuth (1997, section 3.2.1.2). Necessity of the first condition is immediate: if $d = \gcd(c, m) > 1$ and $x_0 = 0$, every term is a multiple of $d$, so at most $m/d$ values are visited.
:::

For $m = 16$: $(a, c) = (5, 3)$ has period 16; $(7, 3)$ fails the third condition and has period 4; $(5, 2)$ fails the first and has period 8.

Python's `random` module uses the Mersenne Twister, of period $2^{19937} - 1$ (Matsumoto and Nishimura, 1998); NumPy's `default_rng` uses PCG64 (O'Neill, 2014) and spawns independent streams from one master seed with `SeedSequence`. Four rules follow:

-   choose one master seed per experiment and record it;
-   derive one stream per worker, split or repetition, never seeding from the clock;
-   seed every library involved: NumPy, PyTorch (`torch.manual_seed`), data-loader workers;
-   report results over several seeds (Proposition 5.6).

```python
import numpy as np

def period(a, c, m, x0=0):
    seen, x, k = {}, x0, 0
    while x not in seen:
        seen[x] = k
        x, k = (a * x + c) % m, k + 1
    return k - seen[x]

print([period(5, 3, 16), period(7, 3, 16), period(5, 2, 16)])   # [16, 4, 8]

def first_draws(master_seed):                       # one master seed, three streams
    children = np.random.SeedSequence(master_seed).spawn(3)
    return [float(np.random.default_rng(s).random()) for s in children]

print([round(x, 4) for x in first_draws(2026)])     # three different streams
print(first_draws(2026) == first_draws(2026))      # True: the same seed gives the same streams
```

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Recursive summation errs by at most $\gamma_{n-1} \sum_i |x_i|$; two orders agree within twice that, but not bit for bit.
-   Threads, GPUs, compiler options and library versions change the order of operations.
-   Kahan summation makes the error almost independent of $n$.
-   A pseudo-random sequence is a function of its seed: record one master seed, spawn streams, report over seeds.
:::

## 7. Software environments, version control and provenance {#ch7}

Code that ran last year may not install today, and a figure may come from a version of the code that nobody can identify. This chapter explains why environments are hard to rebuild, how version control names every state of a project, and how a pipeline knows exactly what to recompute.

### 7.1 Software environments

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Software environment]{.tag} The environment of a computation is everything besides code and data that can change its result: interpreter, libraries and their exact versions, system libraries, compiler, operating system, drivers and hardware.
:::

With **semantic versioning**, a version `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` increases MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for compatible additions and PATCH for fixes. Constraints such as `numpy>=1.24,<2` leave the installer a choice, and choosing well is hard in a precise sense.

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — Installability is NP-complete (Mancinelli et al., 2006)]{.tag} A repository is a finite set of packages, each with dependencies given as a conjunction of disjunctions of packages, and with pairs of conflicting packages. An **installation** contains the dependencies of its members and no conflicting pair. Deciding whether a given package belongs to some installation is NP-complete.

::: proof
*In NP*: an installation is a certificate, checked in polynomial time.

*NP-hard, by reduction from 3-SAT*: for each variable $x_i$, create conflicting packages $x_i^{+}$ and $x_i^{-}$, like two versions of one package.

For each clause $C_j$, create a package $c_j$ depending on the disjunction of the packages of its literals; a target $t$ depends on all the $c_j$.

A satisfying assignment gives an installation: $t$, the $c_j$, and the package matching each variable's value.

Conversely, an installation containing $t$ contains a literal package for each clause. Since $x_i^{+}$ and $x_i^{-}$ conflict, setting $x_i$ true exactly when $x_i^{+}$ is installed satisfies every clause. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Installers therefore use SAT solvers or heuristics, whose answer depends on the solver and on the packages published since: the same requirement file can give different environments on different days. Remedies, from the weakest to the strongest:

-   **pin** exact versions, ideally with file hashes (`pip install --require-hashes`);
-   commit the **lock file** of the package manager, which records the resolved set;
-   ship a **container** image (Docker, Apptainer), which also freezes system libraries;
-   use a **functional package manager** (Nix, Guix), where each package is a function of its exact inputs; `guix time-machine` rebuilds an environment as it was at a past commit of the package collection.

### 7.2 Version control as a Merkle graph

Git names objects by their hash. A **blob** is a file's content; a **tree** lists names, permissions and hashes of blobs and sub-trees; a **commit** holds the hash of a tree, the hashes of its parents, an author, a date and a message.

::: def
[Definition 7.3 — Merkle DAG]{.tag} A Merkle DAG is a DAG whose nodes carry content and are named by the hash of their content together with the names of their children $w_1, \dots, w_r$, in a fixed order (Merkle, 1988):
$$
\mathrm{name}(v) = H\big(\mathrm{content}(v),\ \mathrm{name}(w_1), \dots, \mathrm{name}(w_r)\big).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.4 — A name commits to a whole history]{.tag} If two nodes of Merkle DAGs have the same name, either the sub-DAGs below them are identical, or a collision of $H$ can be read off them.

::: proof
By induction on the height, assuming that the string hashed for a node encodes its content and its child names unambiguously. If the strings hashed for the two nodes differ, they form a collision. Otherwise the nodes have the same content and the same child names, and the induction hypothesis applies to each pair of children. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A commit hash quoted in an article thus identifies every file and the whole history behind a result. Accidental collisions are made negligible by Proposition 0.7. Deliberate collisions of SHA-1, git's hash, became feasible in 2017 (Stevens et al.); git now detects the known attacks and supports SHA-256 repositories.

```python
import hashlib
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

def git_blob(data: bytes) -> str:
    """Name of a file in git: SHA-1 of a header and the content."""
    return hashlib.sha1(b"blob %d\0" % len(data) + data).hexdigest()

print(git_blob(b""))           # e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391, git's empty file
print(git_blob(b"hello\n"))    # equals: echo hello | git hash-object --stdin

def h(*parts: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256("\x1f".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

# A pipeline (Definition 7.5): each step = (code, parameters, inputs)
steps = {
    "data":    ("load v1",    "seed=0",  []),
    "clean":   ("drop NaN",   "",        ["data"]),
    "train":   ("fit ridge",  "lam=0.1", ["clean"]),
    "figure2": ("plot curve", "",        ["train"]),
    "table1":  ("summary",    "",        ["clean"]),
}

def keys(steps):                               # Proposition 7.6: hash in topological order
    order = TopologicalSorter({s: set(d[2]) for s, d in steps.items()}).static_order()
    k = {}
    for s in order:
        code, params, inputs = steps[s]
        k[s] = h(code, params, *[k[i] for i in inputs])
    return k

before = keys(steps)
steps["train"] = ("fit ridge", "lam=0.2", ["clean"])      # change one parameter
after = keys(steps)
print("recompute:", sorted(s for s in steps if before[s] != after[s]))   # ['figure2', 'train']
```

Commit often, tag the version used for each article (`git tag paper-v1`), never rewrite a history others have fetched, and write the commit hash into every result file.

### 7.3 Pipelines and provenance

::: def
[Definition 7.5 — Pipeline]{.tag} A pipeline is a DAG of steps; each step $s$ has code, parameters and input steps $i_1, \dots, i_r$, and produces a target that is a deterministic function of them. Its **key** is computed in a topological order (Proposition 0.5):
$$
\mathrm{key}(s) = H\big(\mathrm{code}_s,\ \mathrm{params}_s,\ \mathrm{key}(i_1), \dots, \mathrm{key}(i_r)\big).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.6 — Content-addressed recomputation is exact]{.tag} Change the code or parameters of one step $s$. Unless $H$ has a collision, the keys that change are exactly those of $s$ and its descendants; every other target can be reused from a cache indexed by keys.

::: proof
In topological order: a step that is neither $s$ nor a descendant of $s$ hashes the same string, so its key is unchanged. The key of $s$ hashes a different string, and so does each descendant, one of whose input keys changed; their keys change unless a collision occurs. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The script checks it: changing the regularisation of `train` recomputes `train` and `figure2`, not `table1`. The classical `make` compares modification times, a weaker criterion; DVC, Nix and Guix index outputs by hashes of their inputs. Next to each result, store a **provenance record**, in the spirit of the W3C PROV model (2013): commit hash, lock file or image digest, command line, seeds, data checksums, hardware and date.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Choosing compatible versions is NP-complete: pin, lock, containerise or use a functional package manager.
-   Git is a Merkle DAG: a commit hash identifies a whole history unless a collision is exhibited.
-   Hashing each step with its inputs' keys recomputes exactly what changed.
-   Store a provenance record with every result.
:::

## 8. Publishing reproducible research: the editorial process {#ch8}

Publishing means passing an editorial process designed before code and data became part of research. This chapter follows a manuscript through it, models the noise of peer review, and describes the venues and identifiers that make code part of the publication.

### 8.1 The editorial process

1.  **Submission**, often after a preprint on arXiv or HAL.
2.  **Desk check** by the editor: scope, format, plagiarism; possible rejection without review.
3.  **Peer review** by two to four reviewers, single-anonymous, double-anonymous or open; conferences add area chairs, a rebuttal and sometimes public reviews on OpenReview.
4.  **Decision** and **revision**: accept, revise or reject; a revision comes with a response letter and a new round.
5.  **Acceptance and contract**: a copyright transfer or a licence to publish (ch. 9.3).
6.  **Production and afterwards**: proofs, the version of record with a DOI, then errata or, for serious errors, retraction.

### 8.2 Peer review as a noisy measurement

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — A Gaussian model of review]{.tag} The quality of a submission is $Q \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. Two independent committees observe
$$
S_A = Q + \varepsilon_A, \qquad S_B = Q + \varepsilon_B, \qquad \varepsilon_A, \varepsilon_B \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2),
$$
with $Q$, $\varepsilon_A$, $\varepsilon_B$ independent, and each accepts the fraction $a$ of best-scored submissions.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — Agreement between committees]{.tag} Let $\rho = 1/(1 + \tau^2)$, let $z_{1-a} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - a)$ (notation of Definition 0.3), and let $\Phi_2(\cdot, \cdot; \rho)$ be the distribution function of a standard bivariate normal pair with correlation $\rho$. Then
$$
\mathbb{P}(B \text{ accepts} \mid A \text{ accepts}) = \frac{\Phi_2(-z_{1-a}, -z_{1-a}; \rho)}{a}.
$$

::: proof
$S_A$ and $S_B$ have variance $1 + \tau^2$ and covariance $\mathrm{Var}(Q) = 1$.

Divided by $\sqrt{1 + \tau^2}$, they form a standard bivariate normal pair $(U, V)$ with correlation $\rho$.

Each committee accepts above $z_{1-a}$, with probability $a$. By the symmetry $(U, V) \mapsto (-U, -V)$, both accept with probability $\Phi_2(-z_{1-a}, -z_{1-a}; \rho)$; divide by $a$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 8.3 — How consistent is acceptance?]{.tag} With an acceptance rate $a = 0.25$:

| Noise $\tau$ | Correlation $\rho$ | $\mathbb{P}(B \text{ accepts} \mid A \text{ accepts})$ |
|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | 0.94 | 0.826 |
| 0.5 | 0.80 | 0.676 |
| 1.0 | 0.50 | 0.481 |
| 2.0 | 0.20 | 0.335 |

When review noise equals the spread of quality ($\tau = 1$), the other committee would reject more than half of the accepted papers.
:::

In the 2014 NeurIPS experiment, part of the submissions went to two independent committees; Cortes and Lawrence (2021) report disagreement on a large share of each committee's accepted papers, of the order of the case $\tau = 1$. Review filters for plausibility and seldom re-executes code: reproducibility must be built into the artefacts.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm, multivariate_normal

def consistency(tau, a):                    # Proposition 8.2
    rho = 1 / (1 + tau**2)
    z = norm.ppf(1 - a)
    both = multivariate_normal(mean=[0, 0], cov=[[1, rho], [rho, 1]]).cdf([-z, -z])
    return both / a

for tau in [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]:
    print(f"tau={tau:4.2f}  rho={1/(1+tau**2):.2f}  P(B | A)={consistency(tau, 0.25):.3f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)              # Monte Carlo check for tau = 1
Q = rng.standard_normal(200_000)
SA, SB = Q + rng.standard_normal(Q.size), Q + rng.standard_normal(Q.size)
accA, accB = SA > np.quantile(SA, 0.75), SB > np.quantile(SB, 0.75)
print(f"simulated: {(accA & accB).sum() / accA.sum():.3f}")
```

### 8.3 Venues that review the code

-   **Artifact evaluation**: the ACM awards badges after reviewing artefacts: *Artifacts Available*, *Artifacts Evaluated* (functional or reusable), *Results Reproduced*, *Results Replicated*.
-   **Checklists**: since its 2019 reproducibility programme (Pineau et al., 2021), NeurIPS asks authors for a checklist on code, data, hyperparameters and statistics.
-   **ReScience C** (Rougier et al., 2017) publishes replications of computational results, with open review of article and code on GitHub.
-   **IPOL**, Image Processing On Line (Limare and Morel, 2011), publishes each article with its source code and an online demonstrator, reviewed together: the reviewer checks that the code implements the algorithm described, and any reader can run it on their own data.

The object under review becomes a triple, text, code and demonstration, and the editorial process gains a step: reviewing the code against the pseudo-code, which ch. 10 prepares.

### 8.4 Identifiers and archives

-   A **DOI** names articles, data and code persistently; Zenodo, run by CERN, archives GitHub releases with a DOI.
-   **Software Heritage** archives public source code under intrinsic, git-compatible SWHIDs: the empty file is `swh:1:cnt:e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391`.
-   **HAL**, the French national open archive, accepts software deposits linked to Software Heritage.
-   **ORCID** identifies authors; a `CITATION.cff` file says how to cite software, following the principles of Smith et al. (2016).
-   The **FAIR** principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016) ask data and software to be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 8

-   A manuscript goes through submission, desk check, review, decision, revision, contract and production.
-   When review noise matches the spread of quality, acceptance is close to a coin flip among good papers.
-   Artifact evaluation, checklists, ReScience C and IPOL review code and data.
-   DOIs, SWHIDs, HAL and `CITATION.cff` make code citable.
:::

## 9. Legal aspects of the code, the article and the data {#ch9}

A reproducibility package bundles code, text and data, which the law treats differently. This chapter explains who owns each, under which terms each can be shared, and when the whole package can be redistributed.

### 9.1 Three objects, three regimes

| Object | Main protection | Typical terms |
|---|---|---|
| Code | copyright (ch. 1.1), possibly patents (ch. 2.6) | free software licences (ch. 2) |
| Article | authors' copyright, often transferred to the publisher | copyright transfer, licence to publish, Creative Commons |
| Data | facts are free; databases have specific rights; personal data are regulated | CC0, CC BY, ODbL, Licence Ouverte, terms of use |

### 9.2 The code: who owns it

-   In France, the economic rights on software created by employees in the exercise of their duties, or following their employer's instructions, belong to the employer (article L113-9 of the Code de la propriété intellectuelle): releasing research code is the institution's decision, often delegated to the laboratory.
-   Unless agreed otherwise, the author of software cannot oppose modifications that harm neither their honour nor their reputation (article L121-7).
-   For students, interns and visitors, it depends on their status and hosting agreement: check it early.

### 9.3 The article

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Versions of an article]{.tag} The **preprint** is the manuscript as submitted; the **accepted manuscript** is the authors' final version after peer review, before the publisher's formatting; the **version of record** is the version published by the publisher.
:::

At acceptance, authors transfer their copyright to the publisher or grant it a licence to publish. In France, the law for a digital republic of 7 October 2016 created a right of open-access deposit, now article L533-4 of the Code de la recherche: for an article from research funded at least half by public funds, the author may make the accepted manuscript freely available after at most 6 months in science, technology and medicine, or 12 months in the humanities and social sciences, even after transferring their rights.

With the **rights retention strategy** of cOAlition S, authors announce at submission that CC BY applies to any resulting accepted manuscript. Creative Commons licences combine BY (attribution), SA (share alike), NC (non-commercial) and ND (no derivatives); only CC BY, CC BY-SA and CC0 allow every reuse, and Creative Commons advises against its licences, CC0 aside, for software.

### 9.4 The data

-   **Facts** are not protected; an original selection or arrangement of them can be.
-   **Databases** in the European Union have a *sui generis* right for 15 years when their making required a substantial investment (Directive 96/9/EC).
-   **Text and data mining** is allowed by Directive (EU) 2019/790 for research organisations on lawfully accessed works (article 3), and for others unless rights holders opt out (article 4).
-   **Personal data** fall under the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), with health data as a special category (article 9) and research rules requiring safeguards such as pseudonymisation (article 89); pseudonymised data remain personal data.
-   **Terms of use** are a contract: data released “for non-commercial research only” cannot be redistributed by their users.

Common data licences are CC0, CC BY 4.0, the Open Database License (a copyleft) and Etalab's Licence Ouverte 2.0.

### 9.5 A redistributable reproducibility package

Stodden (2009) proposed a **Reproducible Research Standard**: text and figures under CC BY, code under a permissive licence such as the modified BSD, data in the public domain, so that the package can be reused with attribution only.

:::: prop
[Proposition 9.2 — When a package can be redistributed]{.tag} Model a package as separately licensed parts placed side by side: code components, texts and data sets. It can be redistributed as a whole if and only if each part may be redistributed under its own terms, and the code components combined into one program are compatible (Definition 2.3).

::: proof
Parts placed side by side form an aggregation: each remains governed by its own terms, which must each allow redistribution. Only code combined into one program forms a combined work, whose distribution must satisfy all its licences at once; by Definition 2.3 and Proposition 2.4, this is the compatibility of its components. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 9.3 — A package with restricted images]{.tag} A package holds MIT code, CC BY figures and images whose terms forbid redistribution. The code and figures may be shared; the images may not. Ship instead a script that downloads them from the official source and verifies their checksums (ch. 7.3), so that others obtain the same files under the original terms.
:::

### 9.6 Models and weights

The legal status of trained weights is unsettled. The OSI's Open Source AI Definition 1.0 (October 2024) requires the freedoms of Definition 1.2 for an AI system, with access to the complete code, the parameters, and sufficiently detailed information about the training data. Models whose weights are published with restrictions of use, often called **open-weight**, are not open source in this sense. The European AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) lightens some obligations for models under free and open-source licences, except general-purpose models with systemic risk; see [Regulating AI](../s2-regulating-ai/index.html).

::: note
[Debate]{.tag} Should publicly funded research software be copyleft, so that improvements return to the public, or permissive, so that industry adopts it? Ex. 15 asks for a dissertation on this question.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 9

-   Code, articles and data have different regimes, and a package must respect each.
-   In France the employer owns the economic rights on employees' software.
-   French law lets authors deposit the accepted manuscript of a publicly funded article after at most 6 or 12 months.
-   Facts are free, databases may carry a 15-year right, personal data fall under the GDPR, terms of use bind users.
-   A package is redistributable when each part allows it and the combined code is compatible.
:::

## 10. Writing a reproducible scientific article {#ch10}

This chapter turns the previous ones into a method for writing. Its central idea: the pseudo-code, the code, the numbers and the figures of an article should be checkable against each other, by the authors first and by any reader afterwards.

### 10.1 Anatomy of a reproducible article

-   **Method**: definitions, then the algorithm in pseudo-code, with every parameter named and given a default value.
-   **Implementation notes**: every deviation of the code from the pseudo-code, such as vectorisation or numerical safeguards.
-   **Experiments**: data and their provenance, protocol, seeds, statistics over repetitions, and the command producing each figure and table.
-   **Limitations**, with failure examples, and an **availability statement** with identifiers (ch. 8.4) and licences (ch. 9).

### 10.2 From pseudo-code to code

::: def
[Definition 10.1 — Faithful implementation]{.tag} An implementation is **faithful** to a pseudo-code when each line of the pseudo-code is mapped to the code implementing it, every deviation is listed and justified in the article, and a test checks that the implementation and a literal transcription of the pseudo-code agree on several inputs.
:::

Otsu's method thresholds a grey-level image into two classes. Let $p_i$ be the proportion of pixels of level $i \in \{0, \dots, 255\}$.

For a threshold $t$, class 0 holds the levels below $t$, with weight $\omega_0$ and mean $\mu_0$; class 1 the others, with weight $\omega_1 = 1 - \omega_0$ and mean $\mu_1$.

::: thm
[Algorithm 10.2 — Otsu's threshold]{.tag}

1.  For $t = 1, \dots, 255$:
2.  split the pixels into levels $< t$ and $\ge t$, and skip $t$ if a class is empty;
3.  compute the between-class variance $\sigma_B^2(t) = \omega_0 \omega_1 (\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2$;
4.  keep the first $t$ that maximises $\sigma_B^2(t)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 10.3 — Two forms of Otsu's criterion]{.tag} Let $\sigma^2$ be the variance of all pixels, $\mu_T$ their mean, and $\mu(t) = \sum_{i<t} i\,p_i$. With $\sigma_k^2$ the variance of the levels in class $k$, define the within-class variance
$$
\sigma_W^2(t) = \omega_0 \sigma_0^2 + \omega_1 \sigma_1^2 .
$$

-   (a) $\sigma^2 = \sigma_W^2(t) + \sigma_B^2(t)$, so maximising $\sigma_B^2$ minimises $\sigma_W^2$.
-   (b) Whenever $0 < \omega_0 < 1$,
$$
\sigma_B^2(t) = \frac{\big(\mu_T\,\omega_0(t) - \mu(t)\big)^2}{\omega_0(t)\,\big(1 - \omega_0(t)\big)} .
$$

::: proof
(a) is the law of total variance for the pixel level given its class: mean of the class variances plus variance of the class means, the latter being $\omega_0 \omega_1 (\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2$.

(b) Since $\mu_T = \omega_0 \mu_0 + \omega_1 \mu_1$ and $\mu(t) = \omega_0 \mu_0$,
$$
\mu_T\,\omega_0 - \mu(t) = \omega_0(\omega_0 - 1)\mu_0 + \omega_0 \omega_1 \mu_1 = \omega_0 \omega_1 (\mu_1 - \mu_0);
$$
square and divide by $\omega_0 \omega_1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Form (b) needs only cumulative sums of the histogram, so all thresholds are evaluated in one pass: a deviation from the literal loop, to be documented and tested.

```python
import numpy as np

def otsu_reference(img):
    """Algorithm 10.2 transcribed literally."""
    best_t, best_var = 0, -1.0
    for t in range(1, 256):                                  # line 1
        low, high = img[img < t], img[img >= t]              # line 2
        if low.size == 0 or high.size == 0:
            continue
        w0, w1 = low.size / img.size, high.size / img.size
        var_b = w0 * w1 * (low.mean() - high.mean()) ** 2    # line 3
        if var_b > best_var:                                 # line 4
            best_t, best_var = t, var_b
    return best_t

def otsu_fast(img):
    """Lines 2-3 for every t at once, by Proposition 10.3 (b): a documented deviation."""
    p = np.bincount(img.ravel(), minlength=256) / img.size
    w0 = np.cumsum(p)[:-1]                                   # omega_0(t), t = 1..255
    m0 = np.cumsum(p * np.arange(256))[:-1]                  # mu(t)
    mT = m0[-1] + 255 * p[255]
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        var_b = (mT * w0 - m0) ** 2 / (w0 * (1 - w0))
    var_b[~np.isfinite(var_b)] = -1.0                        # empty classes are skipped
    return int(np.argmax(var_b)) + 1                         # first maximiser (line 4)

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
for trial in range(3):                                       # test of Definition 10.1
```
